summary: DeltaMCP is a CLI that diffs two OpenAPI spec versions with oasdiff, splits the diff into per-endpoint change units, and asks a LoRA-fine-tuned small code LLM to patch only the affected tools of an existing Python/FastMCP server instead of regenerating the whole server (as AutoMCP does). It is trained on >2000 change samples from Azure Microsoft.Storage specs and evaluated on Microsoft.Resources across five version transitions against AutoMCP.

claims.claim: DeltaMCP uses far less CPU/memory than AutoMCP during updates (~0.1% CPU, ~10.5-12.5 MB vs ~3.0% CPU, ~30 MB).
claims.evidence: Figure 3 only; no table, no variance, no run count. The intro (§1) states memory 'around 12%' vs AutoMCP '±30% memory', while §4 states MB values: the units are inconsistent within the paper. GPU inference cost of the fine-tuned LLM is not reported, so CPU/RAM is not the relevant cost metric.

claims.claim: DeltaMCP touches far fewer tools per update than full regeneration.
claims.evidence: Figure 4; this follows by construction from incremental diffing rather than being an empirical finding.

claims.claim: DeltaMCP's generation quality exceeds/is more consistent than AutoMCP's.
claims.evidence: Figure 5 reports a normalized 100-point composite (syntax compile, 'MCP agent simulations', schema alignment) with no numeric values in text, no definition of the agent simulation, and no indication of which of the three fine-tuned models (StarCoder2-7B, CodeLlama-7B, Phi-3-mini) is used. The abstract gives no number.

claims.claim: DeltaMCP preserves custom enterprise tooling (telemetry, safeguards) that full regeneration discards.
claims.evidence: Asserted in §1/§5/§6; no experiment injects custom code and measures preservation.

patterns.note: Treats MCP servers generated from OpenAPI specs as the agent-to-service integration layer and proposes keeping them in sync incrementally.
Spec (OpenAPI) as source of truth driving regeneration of tooling; evidence weak.
Spec diff between service versions as a contract-change signal for downstream consumers; not evaluated across repos.
LoRA fine-tuning of 7B-class code models on change samples; no comparison against prompting a frontier model.

methodology.sample: One evaluation namespace (Azure Microsoft.Resources), five version transitions; training on >2000 change units from Microsoft.Storage.
methodology.baselines: AutoMCP full regeneration only; no prompted frontier-LLM patching baseline, no deterministic codegen-from-diff baseline (e.g. openapi-generator + merge).
methodology.models: LoRA on StarCoder2-7B, CodeLlama-7B, Phi-3-mini-4k; which one is reported is not stated.
methodology.contamination_controls: Train/eval on different Azure namespaces (Storage vs Resources); same vendor spec style.
methodology.languages: Python (FastMCP) servers only; OpenAPI/Azure specs only.

standards.artifacts: No DeltaMCP code, data, or fine-tuned weights released; only the public Azure spec repo is linked.

biases.detail: Authors define and score their own 100-point composite quality metric with no external check.
CPU/RAM of the orchestration process is reported as the efficiency metric while GPU inference of the fine-tuned model is ignored; 'preserves custom tooling' is never measured.
Figures only; no repeats, no error bars, no numbers in text.
One evaluation namespace, five version transitions.
Sole baseline is full regeneration (AutoMCP), which by construction touches every tool; no incremental baseline with a general LLM.
'self-patching and healing MCP infrastructure', 'revolutionized' with weak evidence.

coi.affiliations: First author Microsoft; two co-authors University of Adelaide.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Uses Microsoft Azure REST API specs as data; DeltaMCP itself is not presented as a Microsoft product; AutoMCP baseline is third-party.
coi.detail: Vendor affiliation and vendor dataset, but not grading a vendor product favorably.

verdict_reason: Interesting problem framing (incremental MCP regeneration from OpenAPI diffs) but the evaluation is figure-only with inconsistent units, no numeric quality results, no variance, one namespace, an undefined quality metric, an unidentified model, a by-construction baseline, and no artifacts. The custom-code-preservation claim is untested.
applicability: The idea is relevant if the Java team exposes its content-delivery REST APIs to agents via MCP: treat the OpenAPI spec as SoT and regenerate tool wrappers from oasdiff output deterministically. But nothing here transfers as evidence: Python/FastMCP only, Azure-only specs, no Java/Spring codegen. For ≥4 ingestion repos a deterministic pipeline (oasdiff breaking-change check in CI per repo + openapi-generator) is a safer spec-driven baseline than a fine-tuned 7B patcher; mixed agent hosts are unaffected since MCP is host-agnostic.
